arc: The teaching describes how a word, born in the interior, is shaped by five organs of the mouth into an audible form that crosses to another's ear — and likens this to a coin minted by five artisans before passing into commerce, so that the descent of truth into a communicable likeness is shown to be a five-fold work of the natural-rational interface.
reading:
This chapter asks what the likeness of the word is — that is, by what correspondence an interior thought becomes something that can be heard by another. The whole teaching is an extended analogy between speech and coinage, both governed by the number five. Its spiritual subject is how truth, conceived inwardly, is shaped through discrete degrees until it can pass between minds as a medium of exchange.

In the first movement the teaching follows a word from its begetting outward. The word is conceived in the interior and comes forth from the mouth so that others hear it. Several organs cooperate in giving it its outward form: the throat (where the breath of perception meets vocal substance), the tongue that spreads it forth, the teeth that cut it, the lips that close it inward, until the word issues outward through the power of these members and is heard from outside. The mouth here is the doorway of expression where interior state crosses into ultimate; the members are the discrete instruments by which a single inward intention is articulated into the differentiated form that the ear can receive. What is being described in correspondence is the descent of a truth from the inmost into the natural — it must be shaped, divided, bounded, and finally released as a likeness of itself before another mind can hear it.

The second movement gives the parable of the coin. One artisan engraves the metal, another engraves further, another cuts it round, another stamps the seal upon it, another forges the body of the blank — five artisans in all who adorn and form the coin. Only after this five-fold work does the coin come into the midst of men and serve as currency, by which they take and give. The five artisans are the five faculties — mind, thought, teaching, counsel, reflection — the complete structure of the natural-rational interface through which truth must be brought before it can pass as a means of exchange. Each artisan represents one discrete degree of formation: one engraves the inmost mark, another the further definition, another bounds it into its proper limit, another seals (imprints the confirmed correspondence), another fashions the bodily blank that will bear all the rest. The coin's "body of the blank" is the ultimate substrate that receives the imprint; the seal is the fixed correspondence that makes it valid currency. Without all five operations, the metal is not yet money and cannot circulate.

The teaching then closes the analogy: just so is it with the word. As it is formed and adorned in the five faculties, so it comes forth and is heard before the ears of others. The point is precisely this: the word that one mind speaks to another is not raw interior substance but a likeness of that substance, minted in five-fold form so that it can travel through the senses. The ear is the receiving end of this currency — the gate of obedient hearing where the imprinted coin is received and counted.

Read spiritually, the chapter is a doctrine about how Divine Truth itself becomes communicable. The Lord's interior good cannot be grasped naked; it descends through the five storehouses, takes its imprint at each degree, and arrives in ultimates as a sealed likeness — a word, a coin, a doctrine — which can then circulate among men as the very medium by which they "take and give" spiritual life. The same five-fold structuring that mints a word in the mouth also mints divine teaching in the soul; the natural exchange of speech is the lowest correspondence of the heavenly exchange of truth between states. Hence the chapter title's emphasis on likeness: what passes between speakers, and between heaven and earth, is never the bare interior but its correspondential likeness, formed by five and sealed for circulation.
title: The Word as Five-Minted Coin: How Truth Becomes Communicable
